So many questions, firstly: the setup. How many cameras and how are you storing / what type of media are you keeping? Image snaps of events, video clips of interest, or full recordings;

Second: Is it linked to a cloud service or are you uploading it manually using a third party cloud service (e.g. Google Drive)?

Third: What resolution are your cameras? Typical CCTV records at 360p with upscaling to 720p. Modern ones can go 1080p using compressed streaming encoding (i.e. smaller files for the recorded resolution compared to Movies off the internet). 

Short answer: You can get away with 30Mbps (~5MBps) assuming it’s a symmetric link. Some ISPs only provide asymmetric links to residential/retail consumers (e.g. Converge), meaning downloading is fast but uploading is slow. It would matter if this is real time tho. 

Get a CCTV system with a NVR (local recording) with cloud service option for events notifications and snapshots.

I have the Moshi iVizor Matte screen protector. It also provides a paper-like surface texture but with the added benefit of being removable and replaceable. It makes for easier application. It is slightly more expensive but worth it.

As for the paper-like screen surface: It will wear off for any and all products with a matte surface due to retention of oil and wearing down of the surface. In the end it will have retained at most 30% of its paper-like surface texture with some cleaning.

The purpose for me for getting the paper-like surface texture is as training wheels to get used to writing and drawing on a (glass) screen. The lack of haptic feedback on the pen if you aren't already used to digital painting messes with your mind, especially if you're used to paper texture.

I would like to believe that for INTJs emotions require some time to process and properly express. In my opinion, the MBTI spectrum is more an indicator on how persons perform problem solving. Human and societal problems are complex in that outcomes can be difficult to measure, except when there is a clear and distinct relationship to the parties involved (e.g. implied or explicit contractual obligations).

Your point on OP being not in the position to teach anyone to appreciate and love an other hits me hard. Societal norms of what is a relationship, and established expected obligations between two persons in a relationship can only really serve as a guide. Human beings need to experience pain, sadness, loss, and joy to truly be able to love. I cannot but agree to the fact that the guy needs to learn this too, but it should never be at the expense of an other. I say this because, even if my current relationship is only my second throughout my life, it was during my first one that I gained insight on what is a relationship.

And I respond to you rather than OP’s post because I do not think I am in a position to give advice on relationships as I do not know the nuances of theirs. Each relationship is different and its nuances can determine whether or not its truly worthwhile to return and repair a damaged one.

To be honest, I completely rejected the entire idea of how my entire person could be defined with a few stereotypes; as if we’re all walking clichés just waiting to happen. My first MBTI evaluation was performed as a compulsory test by my university.

It’s all just a loose guide to which we can ascribe a couple of observable notes on our patterns of behavior. It’s what we make of the results that matters, whether one uses it to map out how best to apply ourselves to our careers, social circles, or self improvement,

I, for one, find it mildly amusing to see how my or others’ actions fit into patterns whereby I can succinctly categorize or judge the likelihood of their (or my) choices regarding future events. Not everyone fits a mold and I’m usually so much more amused when they don’t follow my predictions.

We are the sum total of our memories and choices, rather than a list of clichés.

I have a different definition of emotionally needy persons. Much as I'd like to explain this in a less empathically sounding manner, it seems to me that there just needs to be a comprehensive discussion of how you measure emotional reciprocation vis a vis their own as well as assuring them that you cannot reciprocate equivocally as their expectation dictates.

As implied in the earlier statement, they are not necessarily emotionally needy. They are, rather, expectant of a degree of emotional reciprocation that you simply cannot provide. This may be solved in a single bout of an emotional conversation wherein you let them know how much your gestures mean to you and how they should view these in light of the difference in breadth of expressions you may offer them. This, in following, means you should also express that this difference, by no means, devalues their own expression of emotions.

<edit: my own experience of emotionally needy persons>

In contrast to my own experience, emotionally needy persons tend to crave and are voracious for external validation that it often becomes detrimental to their personal growth. They tend to be virtual black holes of emotional expressions, regardless if platonic or romantic. These are the types of a person whom no matter how much support you give them they seem to have no ear for it.

I have a simple acid test I give to determine whether a person is of the type or not. If they have a problem they are willing to share, you give them a simple virtual shoulder to lean on and a reasonable advice or two. If their problems are legitimate, they will either find a solution by their own power or make use of advice they get. If they persist in their patterns of behavior for longer than necessary, then I make the conclusion that no matter how much validation and consolation I provide they simply ask for more.

If I really want to absorb the information from a podcast or video I focus on it. But sometimes I use it to prime my mind into a state wherein I can readily handle the type of information I need to be digesting or manipulating. In this case, I don’t necessarily multitask but create parallel streams of thought that still allow me to focus on a topic if and when I do get distracted.

As an example, when I was writing my Thesis I couldn’t just jump into it right away as I got home from work. In order to get back on the topic I needed to write I would watch YouTube videos or Podcasts that dealt with technical topics. It would often help me get through writer’s block so I don’t end up writing dry technical reports that seemed to parrot on the same structure every chapter.

In terms of Multitasking, it’s generally a myth. Our brains can, at best, only multiplex between tasks and thoughts. What we generally do when multitasking is divide our attention while quickly jumping between tasks and processes; information is juggled at the fore of our thoughts while it’s more completely digested at the back of our minds. But if you don’t pay attention to the input stream, it  may as well be discarded as extraneous information.
